week.title: The Great AI Rift: Why Meta, Palantir Are Fighting Against OpenAI, Anthropic, Google
week.summary: Jensen Huang's case blends principle with arithmetic. Every downloaded model still needs a GPU to run, and most GPUs are Nvidia's. When Nvidia released the Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model that runs on a ...
highlights: Jensen Huang's case blends principle with arithmetic. Every downloaded model still needs a GPU to run, and most GPUs are Nvidia's. When Nvidia released the Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model that runs on a single GPU in August this year, he said that "Free AI should be great for chips. In March, Nvidia had assembled the Nemotron Coalition, eight labs including Mistral and Perplexity, to build frontier-grade open models. At CES in January, Huang claimed that 80% of startups build on open models. [...] The schism is reshaping how AI gets built. The capability gap that once settled the debate has narrowed sharply: by one widely cited estimate, the best open models now trail the closed frontier by about four months, and cost roughly a third as much per unit of capability. Yet enterprise use of open models has reportedly fallen, as large companies pay a premium for managed services, support, and the very best performance. [...] The line hardened on July 24, when 25 companies, among them Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, signed an open letter titled "Open Weights and American AI Leadership", urging Washington not to restrict open-weight models. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic did not sign. Sam Altman later posted that he wanted America to win in both open and proprietary AI. The hedge was telling: OpenAI released open-weight models in 2025, alarmed by China's progress, but keeps its best systems behind an API.
